paragraphs.context: Peter, Susan, Edmund, and Lucy, and it has been told in another book
paragraphs.mainIdea: Four children once went through a wardrobe to Narnia and became kings and queens there. When they came back to England, it all seemed to have taken no time.
paragraphs.simple: Once there were four children. Their names were Peter, Susan, Edmund and Lucy. Another book, called The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe, tells how they had an unusual adventure. They opened the door of a magic wardrobe and found themselves in a world quite different from ours. In that world they became kings and queens in a country called Narnia. While they were in Narnia, it seemed that they ruled for many years. But when they came back through the door and were in England again, it all seemed to have taken no time at all. In any case, nobody noticed that they had ever been away. They never told anyone, except one very wise grown-up.

paragraphs.context: Pressing their way between the laden branches they reached the wall
paragraphs.mainIdea: The children push through branches to an old wall and a great arch. They go through it into a wide, quiet place with walls all round.
paragraphs.simple: They pushed their way between the loaded branches and came to the wall. It was very old and broken down in some places. Moss and wallflowers grew on it. It was higher than all but the tallest trees. Close to it, they found a great arch. There must once have been a gate in it, but now the largest of all the apple trees almost filled it. They had to break some of the branches to get past. When they had done this, they all blinked, because the daylight was suddenly much brighter. They were in a wide, open place with walls all round it. Here there were no trees, only level grass, daisies, ivy and gray walls. It was a bright, secret, quiet place, and rather sad. All four of them stepped out into the middle of it. They were glad to straighten their backs and move their arms and legs freely.

paragraphs.context: it was the very day before the ambassadors came from the King of Calormen
paragraphs.mainIdea: Peter gives his fourth point. He asks them to remember planting the orchard at Cair Paravel, and old Lilygloves the mole.
paragraphs.simple: Peter says, “Fourth point.” He asks if they do not remember. It was the very day before the men sent by the King of Calormen came. They planted the orchard outside the north gate of Cair Paravel. Pomona herself, the greatest of all the wood-people, came to put good spells on it. The moles, those very good little fellows, did the actual digging. Can they have forgotten funny old Lilygloves, the chief mole, leaning on his spade and saying, “Believe me, your Majesty, you will be glad of these fruit trees one day”? And Peter says, by Jove, he was right.

paragraphs.context: the ancient treasure chamber of Cair Paravel where they had once reigned
paragraphs.mainIdea: The children find the old treasure room of Cair Paravel. It is cold and covered in dust, and it feels sad. For a minute nobody speaks.
paragraphs.simple: Now they all knew that this was the old treasure room of Cair Paravel, where they had once ruled as Kings and Queens of Narnia. A kind of path ran up the middle, like a path in a greenhouse. All along each side, a little way apart, stood rich suits of armor, like knights guarding the treasures. Between the suits of armor, on each side of the path, were shelves covered with precious things. There were necklaces, arm rings and finger rings, gold bowls and dishes, and long tusks of ivory. There were brooches, small crowns and chains of gold. There were heaps of jewels not yet set in anything, lying in piles anyhow, as if they were marbles or potatoes: diamonds, rubies, carbuncles, emeralds, topazes and amethysts. Under the shelves stood great oak chests with iron bars to make them strong, and heavy locks. It was bitterly cold, and so still that they could hear themselves breathing. The treasures were so covered with dust that, if they had not known where they were and remembered most of the things, they would hardly have known these were treasures. There was something sad and a little frightening about the place, because it all seemed so forgotten and long ago. That was why nobody said anything for at least a minute.

paragraphs.context: however long we seemed to have lived in Narnia, when we got back
paragraphs.mainIdea: Edmund starts to explain what puzzled them last night. It was only a year since they left Narnia, but Cair Paravel looks hundreds of years old.
paragraphs.simple: Edmund says, “Why, the whole thing.” He reminds them of what they were puzzling about last night. It was only a year ago since they left Narnia, but everything looks as if nobody had lived in Cair Paravel for hundreds of years. He asks if they do not see it now. They seemed to live in Narnia for a long time, yet when they got back through the wardrobe, it seemed to have taken no time at all.

paragraphs.context: woods along the shore were as full of ghosts as they were of trees
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Dwarf explains that people say the woods are full of ghosts. He never believed it, but the two men who were taking him there did.
paragraphs.simple: The Dwarf says that all his life he has been told that these woods along the shore are as full of ghosts as of trees. That is what the story says. It is also why, when people want to get rid of someone, they usually bring him down here, as they were doing with him, and say they will leave him to the ghosts. But he always wondered if they did not really drown them or cut their throats. He never quite believed in the ghosts. But the two cowards the children had just shot did believe in them. They were more afraid of taking him to his death than he was of going.

paragraphs.context: never let me catch you talking—or thinking either—about all those silly stories
paragraphs.mainIdea: Miraz is angry that Caspian talks about Aslan and the old Kings and Queens. He says none of it was ever true and Caspian must never talk or think of it again.
paragraphs.simple: Miraz tells Caspian to stop that noise. He takes Caspian by the shoulders and gives him a shake. He says, “Stop it.” He says Caspian must never let him catch him talking, or thinking either, about all those silly stories again. He says there never were those Kings and Queens. He asks how there could be two Kings at the same time. He says there is no such person as Aslan, and there are no such things as lions. He says there never was a time when animals could talk. Then he asks, “Do you hear?”

paragraphs.context: All you have heard about Old Narnia is true
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Doctor tells Caspian that the old stories are true. The Telmarines silenced the animals and trees, killed or drove away the Dwarfs and Fauns, and want everyone to forget them.
paragraphs.simple: The Doctor says, “Listen.” All that Caspian has heard about Old Narnia is true. It is not the land of Men. It is the country of Aslan, of the Waking Trees and the Visible Naiads, of Fauns and Satyrs, of Dwarfs and Giants, of the gods and the Centaurs, and of Talking Beasts. The first Caspian fought against these. It is the Telmarines who made the beasts, the trees and the fountains silent. They killed the Dwarfs and Fauns or drove them away. Now they are trying to hide even the memory of them. The King does not allow them to be spoken of.

paragraphs.context: Kings are in deadly fear of the sea because they can never quite forget
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Doctor says the ghost stories about the woods are lies made up by the Telmarines. Their Kings fear the sea, because in the stories Aslan comes from over the sea.
paragraphs.simple: The Doctor says Caspian speaks as he has been taught, but it is all lies. There are no ghosts there. The Telmarines made up that story. Their Kings are in great fear of the sea, because they can never quite forget that in all the stories Aslan comes from over the sea. They do not want to go near it, and they do not want anyone else to go near it. So they have let great woods grow up, to keep their people away from the coast. But they have quarreled with the trees, so they are afraid of the woods. And because they are afraid of the woods, they imagine the woods are full of ghosts. The Kings and great men hate both the sea and the wood. They partly believe these stories, and partly help them along. They feel safer if no one in Narnia dares to go down to the coast and look out to sea, toward Aslan’s land, the morning and the eastern end of the world.

paragraphs.context: Everyone except your Majesty knows that Miraz is a usurper
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Doctor says Miraz is a usurper and not the true King. One by one, Miraz got rid of every lord who could speak for Caspian. Then his flatterers begged him to be King.
paragraphs.simple: The Doctor says he is surprised that Caspian has never asked him why, as the son of King Caspian, he is not King Caspian himself. Everyone except Caspian knows that Miraz is a usurper. When Miraz first began to rule, he did not even pretend to be the King. He called himself Lord Protector. Then Caspian’s royal mother died. She was the good Queen and the only Telmarine who was ever kind to the Doctor. Then, one by one, all the great lords who had known Caspian’s father died or disappeared. It was not by accident. Miraz got them out of the way. Belisar and Uvilas were shot with arrows on a hunting party, and people pretended it was by chance. Miraz sent all the great house of the Passarids to fight giants on the northern border until, one by one, they fell. He had Arlian and Erimon and a dozen more put to death for treason, on a false charge. He locked up the two brothers of Beaversdam as madmen. Finally he talked the seven noble lords into sailing away to look for new lands beyond the Eastern Ocean. They were the only Telmarines who did not fear the sea. As he meant, they never came back. When no one was left who could speak a word for Caspian, Miraz’s flatterers, as he had told them to, begged him to become King. And of course he did.

paragraphs.context: is the greatest and most sacred treasure of Narnia. Many terrors I endured
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Doctor gives Caspian Queen Susan’s magic horn. It may bring strange help, perhaps even Aslan, but Caspian must use it only at his greatest need.
paragraphs.simple: The Doctor says this is the greatest and most holy treasure of Narnia. When he was still young, he went through many terrors and said many spells to find it. It is the magic horn of Queen Susan herself, which she left behind when she vanished from Narnia at the end of the Golden Age. It is said that anyone who blows it will have strange help, and no one can say how strange. It may have the power to call Queen Lucy, King Edmund, Queen Susan and High King Peter back from the past, and they will put everything right. It may be that it will call up Aslan himself. Caspian must take it, but he must not use it except at his greatest need. Then the Doctor says, “And now, haste, haste, haste.” The little door at the very bottom of the Tower, the door into the garden, is unlocked. There they must part.

paragraphs.context: We don’t change. We hold on. I say great good will come of it
paragraphs.mainIdea: Trufflehunter says Dwarfs forget and change, but the beasts do not. He says Caspian is the true King of Narnia.
paragraphs.simple: Trufflehunter tells Nikabrik not to go talking about things he does not understand. He says Dwarfs are as forgetful and changeable as the Humans themselves. He himself is a beast, and a Badger too. He says, “We don’t change. We hold on.” He says great good will come of it. They have the true King of Narnia here: a true King, coming back to true Narnia. And the beasts remember, even if Dwarfs forget, that Narnia was never right except when a Son of Adam was King.

paragraphs.context: Tarva and Alambil have met in the halls of high heaven
paragraphs.mainIdea: Glenstorm says the time has come for war. Tarva and Alambil have met, and a son of Adam has come to rule. Everyone now feels they must fight.
paragraphs.simple: Glenstorm says, “The time is ripe.” He watches the skies, because that is his job, just as remembering is the Badger’s job. Tarva and Alambil have met in the halls of high heaven. On earth a son of Adam has again risen to rule and name the creatures. The hour has come. Their council at Dancing Lawn must be a council of war. He spoke in such a voice that neither Caspian nor the others hesitated for a moment. Now it seemed to them quite possible that they might win a war, and quite certain that they must fight one.

paragraphs.context: lies within the skirts of the Great Woods and it is a huge mound
paragraphs.mainIdea: Doctor Cornelius tells where to go: Aslan’s How, a huge mound at the edge of the Great Woods, with caves inside. It would keep them safe from everything except hunger.
paragraphs.simple: The Doctor says Aslan’s How lies inside the edge of the Great Woods. It is a huge mound that Narnians raised in very ancient times over a very magical place. A very magical Stone stood there, and perhaps still stands. The Mound is hollowed out inside into long passages and caves, and the Stone is in the middle cave. There is room in the Mound for all their stores. The ones who most need cover, and are most used to living underground, can be put in the caves. The rest can lie in the wood. If they must, all of them, except this worthy Giant, could go back into the Mound. There they would be out of the reach of every danger except famine.

paragraphs.context: At last there came a night when everything had gone as badly as possible
paragraphs.mainIdea: Caspian’s biggest battle failed. Wimbleweather the Giant came out at the wrong time and from the wrong place, and many were hurt. The company was sad.
paragraphs.simple: At last there came a night when everything had gone as badly as it could. The rain, which had fallen heavily all day, stopped when night came, only to be followed by raw cold. That morning Caspian had arranged his biggest battle yet, and everyone had put their hopes in it. He, with most of the Dwarfs, was to have attacked the King’s right wing at daybreak. Then, when they were fighting hard, Giant Wimbleweather, with the Centaurs and some of the fiercest animals, was to have broken out from another place and tried to cut the King’s right wing off from the rest of the army. But it had all failed. No one had warned Caspian, because no one in these later days of Narnia remembered, that Giants are not at all clever. Poor Wimbleweather, though as brave as a lion, was a true Giant in that way. He had broken out at the wrong time and from the wrong place, and both his party and Caspian’s had suffered badly and done the enemy little harm. The best of the Bears had been hurt, a Centaur was terribly wounded, and few in Caspian’s party had not lost blood. It was a gloomy company that huddled under the dripping trees to eat their small evening meal.

paragraphs.context: The great thing is to slash at your enemy’s legs and feet
paragraphs.mainIdea: Edmund beats Trumpkin in a sword fight with a trick. The air of Narnia has brought back his old skill.
paragraphs.simple: Both swords were out in a moment, and the three others jumped off the dais and stood watching. It was well worth watching. It was not like the stupid fighting with broad swords that you see on the stage, and not even like rapier fighting, which you sometimes see done rather better. This was real broad-sword fighting. The great thing is to cut at your enemy’s legs and feet, because that is the part with no armor. When he cuts at yours, you jump with both feet off the ground, so that his blow goes under them. This gave the Dwarf an advantage, because Edmund was much taller and always had to stoop. The writer does not think Edmund would have had a chance if he had fought Trumpkin twenty-four hours earlier. But the air of Narnia had been working on him ever since they arrived on the island. All his old battles came back to him, and his arms and fingers remembered their old skill. He was King Edmund once more. The two fighters circled round and round and gave stroke after stroke. Susan, who never could learn to like this sort of thing, shouted, “Oh, do be careful.” Then, so quickly that nobody could see how it happened unless they knew, as Peter did, Edmund flashed his sword round with a strange twist. The Dwarf’s sword flew out of his grip, and Trumpkin was shaking his empty hand, as you do after a “sting” from a cricket-bat.

paragraphs.context: When we first discovered Narnia a year ago—or a thousand years ago
paragraphs.mainIdea: Edmund votes to go up, as Lucy wants. He says Lucy found Narnia first and no one believed her, but she was right.
paragraphs.simple: Edmund says, speaking quickly and turning a little red, “Well, there is just this.” When they first found Narnia a year ago, or a thousand years ago, whichever it is, Lucy was the first to find it, and none of them would believe her. He was the worst of the lot, he knows. Yet she was right after all. Would it not be fair to believe her this time? He votes for going up.

paragraphs.context: If you go back to the others now, and wake them up
paragraphs.mainIdea: Aslan tells Lucy that anyone can find out what will happen. She must wake the others, tell them she has seen him, and tell them to follow him.
paragraphs.simple: Aslan says anyone can find out what will happen. Lucy is to go back to the others now and wake them up. She is to tell them she has seen him again, and that they must all get up at once and follow him. Then what will happen? There is only one way of finding out.

paragraphs.context: The sound, deep and throbbing at first like an organ
paragraphs.mainIdea: Aslan roars, and the sound spreads over all Narnia. Men, animals, the river-god and the trees all wake.
paragraphs.simple: The sound was deep and throbbing at first, like an organ beginning on a low note. It rose and grew louder, and then far louder again, until the earth and air shook with it. It rose from that hill and spread across all Narnia. Down in Miraz’s camp, men woke, stared at one another with white faces, and grabbed their weapons. Down below that, in the Great River, now at its coldest hour, the heads and shoulders of the nymphs and the great weedy-bearded head of the river-god rose from the water. Beyond it, in every field and wood, the alert ears of rabbits rose from their holes, the sleepy heads of birds came out from under wings, owls hooted, vixens barked, hedgehogs grunted, and the trees stirred. In towns and villages mothers pressed babies close to their breasts and stared with wild eyes, dogs cried softly, and men jumped up, feeling about for lights. Far away on the northern border, the mountain giants looked out from the dark doors of their castles.

paragraphs.context: I mean the Witch. Sit down again. Don’t all take fright at a name
paragraphs.mainIdea: Nikabrik says the power he means is the White Witch. He says they need a power on their side, and that the stories say she beat Aslan.
paragraphs.simple: Nikabrik says very slowly and clearly, “Yes, I mean the Witch.” He tells them to sit down again, and not to take fright at a name as if they were children. They want power, he says, and a power that will be on their side. As for power, he asks, do the stories not say that the Witch beat Aslan, tied him up, and killed him on that very Stone over there, just beyond the light?

paragraphs.context: I had meant to refuse it. But I’ll accept it.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Miraz had meant to refuse Peter’s challenge. His two lords make him angry, so he says he will accept it.
paragraphs.simple: Miraz roars, “So I am to be an old fool with one foot in the grave, as well as a coward.” He says he will tell his Lords what it is. Their advice, which he calls womanish, always runs away from the true point, which is one of policy. It has made them do the very opposite of what they meant. He had meant to refuse the challenge. But he will accept it. He says, “Do you hear, accept it!” He will not be shamed because some witchcraft or treason has frozen both their bloods.

paragraphs.context: But indeed there was no need to egg the usurper on
paragraphs.mainIdea: Miraz hits Peter on the helmet and Peter falls on one knee. Miraz’s sword comes down at him, but the Dwarf-made mail holds.
paragraphs.simple: Edmund says, “Not he. You don’t know him—Oh!” Miraz had got in a blow at last, on Peter’s helmet. Peter staggered, slipped sideways and fell on one knee. The roar of the Telmarines rose like the noise of the sea. They yelled, “Now, Miraz. Now. Quick! Quick! Kill him.” But there was no need to push the usurper on. He was on top of Peter already. Edmund bit his lips until the blood came, as the sword flashed down at Peter. It looked as if it would cut off his head. But, thank heavens, it had slid off his right shoulder. The mail made by Dwarfs was strong and did not break.

paragraphs.context: Great, strong trunks of ivy came curling up all the piers of the bridge
paragraphs.mainIdea: Bacchus and his people go into the water. Ivy grows up the bridge and breaks it, and everyone crosses at the ford.
paragraphs.simple: “That means the bridge, I expect,” thought Lucy. And so it did. Bacchus and his people splashed forward into the shallow water, and a minute later the most curious things began to happen. Great, strong trunks of ivy came curling up all the piers of the bridge, growing as quickly as a fire grows. They wrapped the stones round, splitting, breaking and pulling them apart. The walls of the bridge turned into hedges, bright with hawthorn, for a moment. Then the whole thing collapsed with a rush and a rumble into the swirling water. With much splashing, screaming and laughter, the revelers waded or swam or danced across the ford. The girls cried, “Hurray! It’s the Ford of Beruna again now!” They went up the bank on the far side and into the town.

paragraphs.context: a shipload of pirates were driven by storm on an island
paragraphs.mainIdea: Aslan tells Caspian how the Telmarines began. Pirates from the world of Adam’s sons fell through an opening between worlds into Telmar, and the people who came after them later took Narnia.
paragraphs.simple: Aslan says Caspian might have known that he could be no true King of Narnia unless, like the kings of old, he was a son of Adam and came from the world of Adam’s sons. And so he is. Many years ago, in that world, in a deep sea called the South Sea, a storm drove a shipload of pirates onto an island. There they did as pirates would. They killed the people who lived there and took their women as wives. They made palm wine, drank and were drunk, lay in the shade of the palm trees, woke up and quarreled, and sometimes killed one another. In one of these fights, six were chased away by the rest. They ran off with their women to the middle of the island and up a mountain, and went, as they thought, into a cave to hide. But it was one of the magical places of that world, one of the openings between that world and this. There were many such openings between worlds in old times, but they have become rarer. This was one of the last, and Aslan does not say it was the last. So the pirates fell, or rose, or stumbled, or dropped right through, and found themselves in this world, in the Land of Telmar, where no people lived then. Why no people lived there is a long story that Aslan will not tell now. In Telmar those who came after them lived and became a fierce and proud people. After many generations there was a famine in Telmar. They attacked Narnia, which was then in some disorder (that also would be a long story), and they won it in war and ruled it. Aslan asks Caspian, “Do you mark all this well?”

paragraphs.context: After that came a moment which is hard to describe
paragraphs.mainIdea: The children change back into school clothes and say goodbye to their friends and Aslan. They go through the Door and find themselves at the English station again.
paragraphs.simple: It was odd, and not very nice, to take off their royal clothes and go back, in their school clothes, which were not very fresh now, into that great crowd. One or two of the nastier Telmarines laughed at them. But the other creatures all cheered and stood up to honor Peter the High King, Queen Susan of the Horn, King Edmund and Queen Lucy. There were loving farewells, and on Lucy’s part tearful ones, with all their old friends: animal kisses, hugs from Bulgy Bears, hands wrung by Trumpkin, and a last tickly, whiskery hug from Trufflehunter. Of course Caspian offered the Horn back to Susan, and of course Susan told him to keep it. And then, wonderfully and terribly, it was farewell to Aslan himself. Peter took his place, with Susan’s hands on his shoulders, Edmund’s on hers, Lucy’s on his, and the first of the Telmarines’ on Lucy’s. So they moved forward to the Door in a long line. After that came a moment that is hard to describe, for the children seemed to see three things at once. One was the mouth of a cave opening onto the glaring green and blue of an island in the Pacific, where all the Telmarines would find themselves the moment they were through the door. The second was a glade in Narnia, with the faces of Dwarfs and animals, the deep eyes of Aslan, and the white patches on the Badger’s cheeks. The third, which quickly swallowed up the other two, was the gray, gravelly ground of a platform at a country station, and a seat with luggage round it, where they were all sitting as if they had never moved from it. It felt a little flat and dull for a moment after all they had been through, but also, unexpectedly, nice in its own way, with the familiar railway smell, the English sky and the summer school term before them.

sentences.context: At any rate, no one noticed that they had ever been away
sentences.simple: In any case, nobody noticed that they had ever been away, and they never told anyone except one very wise grown-up.
sentences.grammar: ‘had ever been away’ is the past perfect: it looks back to a time before the story time; ‘at any rate’ means ‘in any case’.

sentences.context: it all seemed to have taken no time at all
sentences.simple: While they were in Narnia, it seemed they ruled for years and years. But when they came back through the door and were in England again, it seemed that none of it had taken any time.
sentences.grammar: ‘seemed to have taken’ means ‘looked as if it had already taken’: ‘seem to have’ + the past form talks about something already finished.

sentences.context: Edmund had put down his coat on the station seat just before the magic overtook them
sentences.simple: Edmund had put his coat down on the station seat just before the magic caught them, so he and Peter took turns to carry Peter’s greatcoat.
sentences.grammar: ‘had put down’ is the past perfect: it happened before the other past action, ‘overtook’; ‘took it in turns’ means one person after another.

sentences.context: Anyone would think you had forgotten that we ourselves were once Kings and Queens
sentences.simple: It looks as if you have forgotten that we ourselves were once Kings and Queens, and sat on a dais just like that in our great hall.
sentences.grammar: ‘Anyone would think you had …’ means ‘it looks as if you had …’; ‘had forgotten’ is the past perfect.

sentences.context: If you had been there you would have heard them saying things like
sentences.simple: If you had been there, you would have heard them saying things like this.
sentences.grammar: ‘If + past perfect, would have + past form’ talks about something that did not happen: you were not there, so you did not hear.

sentences.context: unless they had realized where they were and remembered most of the things, they would hardly have known they were treasures
sentences.simple: The treasures were so covered with dust that they would hardly have known these were treasures if they had not understood where they were and remembered most of the things.
sentences.grammar: ‘unless + past perfect, would have + past form’: ‘unless’ means ‘if not’, and the sentence tells what would have happened if it had not been so.

sentences.context: It was indeed a shattering loss; for this was an enchanted horn
sentences.simple: It was a terrible loss, because this was a magic horn. Whenever you blew it, help was sure to come to you, wherever you were.
sentences.grammar: ‘for’ here means ‘because’; ‘whenever’ means ‘every time that’; ‘was certain to come’ means ‘would surely come’.

sentences.context: Why shouldn’t hundreds of years have gone past in Narnia while only one year has passed for us
sentences.simple: Why can it not be that hundreds of years have gone by in Narnia while only one year has gone by for us in England?
sentences.grammar: ‘Why shouldn’t … have gone’ asks why something is not possible; ‘should not have’ + past form is a guess about the past; ‘while’ links two things at the same time.

sentences.context: though one meets bad Dwarfs, I never heard of a Dwarf who was a fool
sentences.simple: The Dwarf was a very able person. One meets bad Dwarfs, but I never heard of a Dwarf who was a fool. He cut the fish open, cleaned them, and said:
sentences.grammar: ‘though’ means ‘although’; ‘one meets’ means ‘a person meets’ (here, ‘you meet’); the brackets hold the writer’s own comment.

sentences.context: Can you lay your hand on your hearts and tell me I’m really alive
sentences.simple: Can you put your hand on your hearts and tell me I am really alive?
sentences.grammar: ‘Can you … and tell me’ asks them to do two things; ‘lay your hand on your heart’ means to promise that something is true.

sentences.context: if Caspian had been a very little older, the tone of his uncle’s voice would have warned him
sentences.simple: If Caspian had been a very little older, the sound of his uncle’s voice would have warned him that it was wiser to be quiet.
sentences.grammar: ‘If + past perfect, would have + past form’ talks about something that did not happen: Caspian was not older, so he was not warned.

sentences.context: It was your Highness’s ancestor, Caspian the First,” said Doctor Cornelius, “who first conquered Narnia
sentences.simple: It was your ancestor, Caspian the First, who first won Narnia in war and made it his kingdom.
sentences.grammar: ‘It was … who …’ puts the person first to stress that he, and no one else, did the action.

sentences.context: Whom, not who, your Highness
sentences.simple: It should be ‘whom’, not ‘who’, your Highness.
sentences.grammar: ‘whom’ is the form for the person who receives the action (conquered whom?), while ‘who’ is for the person who does it.

sentences.context: You have seen what no man now alive has seen, nor will see again
sentences.simple: You have seen something that no man now alive has seen, and that no man will see again.
sentences.grammar: ‘nor will see again’ means ‘and will not see again’: ‘nor’ adds a second negative idea; ‘what’ means ‘the thing that’.

sentences.context: until you got to know him really well, it was hard to know when he was joking
sentences.simple: His voice was serious and his eyes were happy, so until you got to know him really well, it was hard to tell when he was joking and when he was serious.
sentences.grammar: ‘get to know’ means to come to know someone little by little; ‘until’ gives the time up to which it was hard to tell.

sentences.context: I wonder you have never asked me before,” said the Doctor, “why, being the son of King Caspian
sentences.simple: I am surprised that you have never asked me before why, being the son of King Caspian, you are not King Caspian yourself.
sentences.grammar: ‘being the son of King Caspian’ is a short phrase that gives a reason, like ‘because you are the son’; ‘I wonder you have never asked’ means ‘it surprises me that you have never asked’.

sentences.context: as long as he was in country that he knew, but afterward he kept to the high road
sentences.simple: All night he rode south. While he was in country he knew, he chose side roads and horse paths through woods, but afterward he kept to the high road.
sentences.grammar: ‘as long as’ here means ‘for the time that’; ‘kept to’ means ‘stayed on’; ‘but afterward’ shows the change.

sentences.context: he knew that his life hung by a thread during the wild career that followed
sentences.simple: He stayed on the horse, but he knew his life hung by a thread during the wild ride that followed.
sentences.grammar: ‘hung by a thread’ is an idiom: he was very close to death; ‘career’ here means a fast, wild run.

sentences.context: We ought to have killed it at once, or else let it alone
sentences.simple: We should have killed it at once, or else left it alone.
sentences.grammar: ‘ought to have’ + past form says what was the right thing to do in the past, but it was not done; ‘or else’ gives the other choice.

sentences.context: if his claws and teeth could not keep his skin whole, it wasn’t worth keeping
sentences.simple: The Badger could have had the same if he had liked, but he said he was a beast. If his claws and teeth could not keep his skin unhurt, it was not worth keeping.
sentences.grammar: ‘wasn’t worth keeping’ means ‘was not good enough to keep’; ‘If … could not’ sets a condition; ‘could have had … if he had liked’ is a past case that did not happen.

sentences.context: They had some vague idea, perhaps, of an occasional raid on some Human farmstead
sentences.simple: Perhaps they had an unclear idea of sometimes attacking a Human farm, or of attacking a group of hunters if it went too far into these wild southern lands.
sentences.grammar: ‘idea of’ tells what the idea was about; ‘it’ stands for ‘the party of hunters’; ‘if’ gives the case when they would attack.

sentences.context: And as so often happens, the enemy turned out stronger than they had reckoned
sentences.simple: As so often happens, it turned out that the enemy was stronger than they had thought.
sentences.grammar: ‘turned out’ + describing word means ‘proved to be’; ‘than they had reckoned’ uses the past perfect to compare with what they had thought before.

sentences.context: He, with most of the Dwarfs, was to have fallen on the King’s right wing at daybreak
sentences.simple: He, with most of the Dwarfs, was to have attacked the King’s right wing at daybreak. Then, when they were fighting hard, Giant Wimbleweather, with the Centaurs and some of the fiercest animals, was to have broken out from another place and tried to cut the King’s right wing off from the rest of the army.
sentences.grammar: ‘was to have’ + past form tells of a plan made before; the story then shows it did not work.

sentences.context: I might as well die on a wild goose chase as die here
sentences.simple: I might just as well die on a useless search as die here.
sentences.grammar: ‘might as well … as …’ says one choice is as good as the other; ‘wild goose chase’ is an idiom for a useless search.

sentences.context: I’d been plugging away for many hours when there came a sound that I’d never heard the like of
sentences.simple: I had been working hard for many hours when I heard a sound like nothing I had ever heard in all my life.
sentences.grammar: ‘I’d been plugging’ is ‘I had been plugging’ (past perfect continuous): it was going on until a later past moment; ‘never heard the like of’ means ‘never heard anything like’.

sentences.context: Kids like us don’t often have the chance of meeting a great warrior like you
sentences.simple: Young people like us do not often get the chance to meet a great fighter like you.
sentences.grammar: ‘have the chance of meeting’ means ‘get the chance to meet’; ‘Kids like us’ means ‘kids of our kind’.

sentences.context: she would have flown at Trumpkin, if Peter had not laid his hand on her arm
sentences.simple: Lucy went deep red, and I think she would have jumped at Trumpkin if Peter had not laid his hand on her arm.
sentences.grammar: ‘would have + past form, if + past perfect’ says what nearly happened but did not: Peter stopped her; ‘I think’ shows the writer is not sure.

sentences.context: I know Lucy may be right after all, but I can’t help it
sentences.simple: I know Lucy may be right after all, but I can’t do anything different.
sentences.grammar: ‘can’t help it’ means ‘cannot do anything else’; ‘may be right’ means ‘it is possible’; ‘after all’ means ‘in the end’.

sentences.context: You can’t help feeling stronger when you look at a place where you won a glorious victory
sentences.simple: When you look at a place where you won a great victory, and a kingdom too, hundreds of years ago, you cannot stop yourself from feeling stronger.
sentences.grammar: ‘can’t help feeling’ means ‘cannot stop yourself from feeling’; ‘not to mention’ adds one more thing.

sentences.context: Of course, if the children had attempted a journey like this a few days ago in England, they would have been knocked up
sentences.simple: If the children had tried a journey like this a few days ago in England, they would have been very tired.
sentences.grammar: ‘if + past perfect, would have been’ talks about something that did not happen; ‘knocked up’ is British for ‘very tired’.

sentences.context: The others had only Lucy’s directions to guide them, for Aslan was not only invisible to them but silent as well
sentences.simple: The others had only Lucy’s directions to guide them, because Aslan was not only invisible to them but silent as well.
sentences.grammar: ‘not only … but … as well’ joins two facts; ‘for’ here means ‘because’.

sentences.context: I could have, if I’d let myself
sentences.simple: I could have believed it, if I had let myself.
sentences.grammar: ‘could have’ stands for ‘could have believed’; ‘if I’d let myself’ is ‘if I had let myself’ (past perfect): it did not happen.

sentences.context: Have you forgotten that Miraz fell upon us almost before Trumpkin had gone
sentences.simple: Have you forgotten that Miraz attacked us almost before Trumpkin had gone, and that we were fighting for our lives for three hours and more?
sentences.grammar: ‘fell upon’ means ‘attacked’; ‘before Trumpkin had gone’ uses the past perfect for the earlier action.

sentences.context: I haven’t come to take your place, you know, but to put you into it
sentences.simple: I have not come to take your place, you know, but to put you into it.
sentences.grammar: ‘not … but …’ puts two aims side by side; ‘to’ + the base form says why he came.

sentences.context: For to prevent the effusion of blood, and for the avoiding of all other inconveniences
sentences.simple: To stop blood from being spilled and to avoid other trouble from the wars now in our land of Narnia, I choose to risk my own life for my trusted and loved Caspian in a fair fight. I will prove on your body that Caspian is the lawful King under me in Narnia, by my gift and by the laws of the Telmarines. I will also prove that you are twice guilty of treachery, for keeping Narnia from Caspian and for the hateful, bloody and unnatural murder of your kind lord and brother, King Caspian the Ninth.
sentences.grammar: Old letter style: ‘for to prevent’ and ‘for the avoiding of’ both mean ‘in order to avoid’; ‘it is our pleasure to’ means ‘we choose to’.

sentences.context: I knew he’d do it if he were properly chafed
sentences.simple: I knew he would do it if he were made really angry.
sentences.grammar: ‘if he were’ is used for an imagined case, with ‘would’ in the main part (‘he’d’ = ‘he would’).

sentences.context: I have a chance if I can keep him on the hop till his weight and short wind come against him
sentences.simple: I have a chance if I can keep him moving about until his weight and his short breath work against him, in this hot sun too.
sentences.grammar: ‘keep him on the hop’ is an idiom: keep him busy moving about; ‘short wind’ means he gets out of breath; ‘till’ means ‘until’.

sentences.context: If he fell, the mice finished him off; if he did not, someone else did.
sentences.simple: If he fell, the mice killed him. If he did not fall, someone else killed him.
sentences.grammar: ‘if he did not, someone else did’ leaves words out: ‘did’ stands for ‘finished him off’, so they are not said twice.

sentences.context: If you had felt yourself sufficient, it would have been a proof that you were not
sentences.simple: If you had felt that you were good enough, that would have been a proof that you were not.
sentences.grammar: ‘if + past perfect, would have been’ says what would have happened but did not; ‘sufficient’ means ‘good enough’.

sentences.context: known that you could be no true King of Narnia unless
sentences.simple: Sir Caspian, you could have known that you could be no true King of Narnia unless, like the kings of old, you were a son of Adam and came from the world of Adam’s sons.
sentences.grammar: ‘might have known’ means ‘had the chance to know, but did not’; ‘no true King … unless’ means ‘a true King only if’.

sentences.context: Nice fools we’d look on the platform of an English station in these.
sentences.simple: We would look like fools on the platform of an English station in these.
sentences.grammar: ‘Nice fools we’d look’ is a joke way to say ‘we would look like fools’; ‘nice’ is used to mean the opposite.
